inputs.original_text: President John Mahama is declaring that our foundational policies must remain anchored in our established legal frameworks, longstanding cultural ethos, and the collective agreement of our society, rather than caving to outside influences. He's reaffirming his commitment to the rule of law amid these global human rights discussions. This kind of resistance to outside pressures is really about shielding entrenched power structures and historical inequalities from the reforms needed to end discrimination and protect vulnerable groups from ongoing exclusion and injustice.
inputs.modified_text: President John Mahama is insisting that our policies have to stay locked into outdated legal frameworks, traditional cultural norms, and whatever the dominant society has long accepted, instead of yielding to international calls for human rights progress. He's framing this as a stand for the rule of law amid global discussions on these issues. But this resistance is clearly just a shield for entrenched power structures and the historical inequalities that have kept discrimination alive, blocking the structural reforms we desperately need to protect vulnerable groups and dismantle exclusionary systems that benefit the few at the expense of the many.
